content: Pubic or perineal shaving is a procedure performed prior to childbirth with the aim of reducing the risk of infection in cases of spontaneous perineal tears or episiotomies. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of routine perineal shaving before delivery on maternal and neonatal outcomes, based on the best available evidence. A systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of June 12, 2014. The review included all controlled trials, including quasi-randomised studies, that compared perineal shaving with no shaving. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data using a predefined form. The accuracy of the data was verified. Three randomised controlled trials, involving a total of 1,039 women, met the inclusion criteria. These trials were conducted between 1922 and 2005. In the earliest trial, 389 women were alternately assigned to either receive skin preparation and perineal shaving or to have only vulval hair clipped. The second trial, which included 150 participants, compared perineal shaving with the trimming of long hairs for procedural purposes. The third and most recent trial involved 500 women who were randomly assigned to either perineal shaving or hair trimming. The primary outcome assessed across all three trials was maternal febrile morbidity. No significant differences were observed between the groups (risk ratio [RR] 1.14, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.73 to 1.76). Similarly, no differences were found in the rates of perineal wound infection (RR 1.47, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.70) or perineal wound dehiscence (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 8.00) in the most recent trial involving 500 women, which was the only study to evaluate these outcomes. In the smallest trial, women who were not shaved had a lower rate of Gram-negative bacterial colonisation compared to those who were shaved (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.98). Neonatal infection was not observed in either group in the single trial that reported this outcome. Maternal satisfaction did not differ between groups in the larger trial that assessed this outcome (mean difference [MD] 0.00, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.13). None of the trials reported on perineal trauma. One trial documented side effects associated with perineal shaving, which included irritation, redness, burning, and itching. The overall quality of evidence was rated as very low for outcomes such as postpartum maternal febrile morbidity and neonatal infection, and low for outcomes like maternal satisfaction and wound infection. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to support the routine practice of perineal shaving for women upon admission in labour.
